title: How a retry is applied to a method
summary: Framework 7 wires retry the same way as everything else: an annotation, an @Import, a BeanPostProcessor, an interceptor. The spec object in the middle is where the backoff arithmetic lives.
entry: Put a breakpoint in AbstractRetryInterceptor.invoke on a bean with @Retryable and call a failing method. Every attempt after the first re-enters from the retry loop, not from your caller.

steps.notice: The switch, new in Framework 7. Read its attributes: order defaults to LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 1, which places retry outside most other advice, so a retried call re-runs the transaction rather than retrying inside it.

Registers the two post-processors, retryAdvisor and concurrencyLimitAdvisor, under internal* bean names. Same shape as @EnableScheduling and @EnableAsync; once you have seen it three times you can predict where any feature lives.

Adds the retry advisor to any bean carrying the annotation, which is where your bean becomes a proxy and self-invocation stops working. It also takes an ApplicationEventPublisher, so retries can be observed as MethodRetryEvent rather than only logged.
The loop. Read how the initial call is counted: maxRetries is retries AFTER the first attempt, so maxRetries = 2 means the method runs three times.
The resolved policy for one method: includes, excludes, predicate, delay, multiplier, jitter and maxDelay, already parsed from the annotation.
The extension point when includes and excludes are not enough - for example retrying only on a particular SQL state or HTTP status.
The programmatic equivalent, also new in Framework 7 and in spring-core rather than spring-context. Use it where an annotation cannot reach, such as inside a lambda or a self-call.
The other half of the package. @ConcurrencyLimit bounds how many callers may be inside a method at once, blocking the rest rather than rejecting them.
